job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, I say a quick prayer, and I'm in the office at a regional bank in San Antonio by eight. I'm a junior developer on the team that looks after the app customers use to check balances and pay bills. I fix small bugs, write tests and sit in on the stand-up meeting, where I mostly listen. At lunch I call my mother, and after work I go to my cousin Daniela's place, where I rent the spare room, and we cook together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about how you got here.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was the first in my family to go to university. I did computer science at a state university here in Texas and finished with a good result. My final project was a scheduling app for a parish food bank, and I did a summer internship at the bank, which is how I got the job. My mother cleans offices at night and my father drives a truck. I send them about two hundred dollars a month, I owe around ten thousand, and I have about six weeks of costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because I've learned that big promises usually shrink when you look closely. At work I'd say the tools help with small things, like writing a test, and my team lead is happy with that. At church people would just ask if I'm still happy at the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay, but I'd be lying if I said I'm relaxed. I send money home every month, so if anything happened to my job, my parents would feel it too. Banks are steady, but my team is small, and I'm one of the newest people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard and not complain. I'd try to get one extra certification, like the cloud one the bank pays for, because the bank rewards that. I'd keep sending the two hundred and try to raise my savings to three months. I'd also keep helping at the parish food bank, since I built the app and the volunteers like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay. A bit of a weight on the shoulders, but a familiar one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if your job goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would work extra nights, which she already does too many of, and my father would take longer routes. They'd never ask me for anything, and that's what makes me feel it. I'd go back to Daniela's sofa and apply anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bank is steady. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People have used banks for hundreds of years, and customers like to see a person if something goes wrong. The bank has been hiring juniors every year since I started. It isn't a promise, but it's more than a startup could give me.

The tools help with **small things**, like writing a test.
think: I send money home, so if my job went, **my parents** would feel it too.
My team is small, and I'm one of the **newest** people.
do: Keep sending **two hundred dollars** and build savings to three months.
Keep helping at the parish **food bank**.
feel: **Fairly okay**, with a familiar weight on the shoulders.

fieldNote: Money sent home makes her job a **family** matter.
Steady and practical: she takes the bank-paid course.
Her quiet faith shows in her **routine** more than her words.

steps.text: Pass the cloud certification the bank pays for
Keep sending 200 dollars home and raise savings to three months
Keep volunteering on the parish food bank app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be sensible about it. At work I'd say let's try the tools on low-risk jobs first and keep people checking. At church I'd say the old rule still applies: do good work and look after your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. In a bank, the junior developer jobs are simple fixes and test writing, and those are what AI does in minutes. If my team shrinks from eight to six, I could be one of the two. I'd also be sending money home with less certainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools every day at work, carefully, and learn what they can't do well, like handling money and rules. I'd ask my lead to put me on the compliance side, since banking rules need careful humans. I'd keep sending the two hundred, but I'd say to my parents we should be ready to cut it. And I'd take on a part-time weekend job helping a small firm with their website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, and then I pray and it loosens a bit. I try not to bring it to my mother, because she worries too much already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why compliance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a bank gets fined if a rule is wrong, and someone has to sign for it. I'd like to be that person, with a name and a desk. The tool can read the rules, but a person has to be responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your parents about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my father, not my mother. He'd say it's fine, we manage. But I'd see him go quiet at the kitchen table, because he feels it's his job to look after me, not the other way round.

say: Let's be sensible: try the tools on **low-risk** jobs and keep people checking.
The old rule still applies: **do good work** and look after family.
think: Simple fixes and test writing are what AI does in **minutes**.
If my team shrinks from eight to six, I could be **one of two**.
do: Use AI tools **every day** and learn what they can't do.
Take a weekend job building a small firm's **website**.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, then it loosens when I pray.

fieldNote: Looks for the role with **responsibility** attached: compliance.

steps.text: Use an AI coding tool daily and log where it fails

Build a website for a small firm on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down, and our leaders need to take responsibility. At work I'd keep my head down and watch what the bank plans, but I'd hope for an honest talk. At church, I'd ask people to pray and to look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm very afraid. A bank's work is mostly thinking work, and AI that does it better and cheaper means far fewer people. My parents depend on some of my money, and their jobs, cleaning and driving, will last longer, but robots arrive about three years later. I'd feel everything I worked for was a ladder that's being pulled up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything except rent and food, and save as hard as I can. I'd tell my parents at once, so they could plan. I'd talk to the priest and to my uncle, who owns a small taqueria, about some work there in an emergency. I'd also apply to the government and city offices that still hire people to deal with people. And I'd ask Daniela if we could look for a cheaper place together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd feel scared and also ashamed, like I let everyone down. I'd lie awake counting how many weeks I could pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my family sacrificed for me to go to university and get a safe job. If it goes in two years, it feels like I wasted their sacrifice. I know that's not fair, and my mother would say so, but the feeling is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mother say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, mija, we have survived worse. She'd put a bowl of food in front of me and tell me to eat. And then she'd say we'd work it out, and I'd believe her for about an hour.

say: We need to **slow down**, and leaders need to take responsibility.
At church I'd ask people to **pray** and look out for each other.
think: A bank's work is mostly thinking work, so **far fewer** people would be needed.
Everything I worked for feels like a **ladder** being pulled up.
do: Spend only on **rent and food** and save hard.
Tell my parents at once, so they can **plan**.
Look for work at my uncle's **taqueria** and city offices.
feel: **Scared and ashamed**, lying awake counting weeks of bills.
S2.quote: My family sacrificed for me to go to university and get a safe job. If it goes in two years, it feels like I wasted their sacrifice.
fieldNote: Her fear is wrapped in **shame** about her family's sacrifice.
Turns to **faith**, family and the community network first.
Honest that her mother's comfort works for only about an hour.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent and food
Tell my parents at once so they can plan
Ask my uncle about shifts at his taqueria
Move into a cheaper place with my cousin Daniela

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to prepare, and people should use it. At work I'd ask what training the bank would offer, and at church I'd say we should prepare the young people for different work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be afraid but not helpless. By 2031 I'd be 27 and have five years in banking, and maybe I'd be the person who checks the AI. But I'd still have to make sure my parents are safe, which is the thing I think about most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save aggressively and try to have a year of costs in the bank by 2031. I'd help my parents buy a small house or pay down their debt, if I can, so they aren't exposed. I'd use the bank's training to move into risk or compliance. I'd also go to evening classes on the people side of banking, like customer service and rules, because that's where they'd still need humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit afraid, but I'd also feel useful, because there's something to do. I'm better when I have a job in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your parents with the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents rent from a man who raises the rent every year. If I put a deposit down on a house for my parents, even a small one, they'd have something no technology can take. It might take three years, and my father would argue with me about taking the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that slow your own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd marry later, maybe. I don't have a boyfriend now, but I'd want the family safe first. My mother says that's the wrong order, but it's how I feel.

I'd ask the bank what **training** it would offer.

What I think about most is keeping my **parents** safe.

fieldNote: Plans around her **parents'** security rather than her own.
Willing to delay her **own** life, against her mother's advice.
Prefers the human side of banking: rules and customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, because it gives us time to adjust. At work I'd suggest we plan how to train juniors in a world with AI. At church I'd say we pray, plan and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly calm. I'd be 32, probably a senior developer or a team lead, maybe married with a child. I'd still worry about my parents getting older, but I'd have time to help them. I'd keep my feet on the ground and not assume it will go well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the bank and aim for team lead in six or seven years. I'd put money into a small house for my parents and a retirement account for me. I'd use AI tools as part of my job, and I'd try to learn some of the newer systems. I'd also keep volunteering with the parish food bank, since they'd need software help more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, hopeful. I'd feel I could plan a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'plan a life' mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means thinking about getting married, a house, children, and a job that I like. In the two-year world I don't plan at all. In this one I can write it in a notebook and light a candle for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a danger in feeling hopeful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, believing that the date is fixed. It could come sooner. So I'd keep a small emergency fund and keep learning, even when everything feels fine.

say: Ten years is a **blessing**, because it gives us time to adjust.
I'd say we **pray, plan and work**.
think: I'd be 32, perhaps **team lead**, maybe married with a child.
I'd still worry about my parents **getting older**, but have time to help.
do: Stay at the bank and aim for **team lead** in six or seven years.
Put money into a **house for my parents** and a retirement account.
Keep volunteering with the **parish food bank**.
feel: **Calm and hopeful**, as if I could plan a life.
S4.quote: In the two-year world I don't plan at all. In this one I can write it in a notebook and light a candle for it.
fieldNote: Time lets her plan **marriage and children**, which she avoids otherwise.
Hope is cautious: she keeps an **emergency fund**.

steps.text: Work towards team lead at the bank in six or seven years
Put a deposit on a small house for my parents
Open a retirement account and pay in monthly
Keep an emergency fund of three months of costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to look after my parents and my own future together. What would help is a bank that is honest early, training I don't have to pay for, and neighbours and church who'd stand together. I'd also like government help that is quick and respectful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that a lot of people my age are carrying a family, not just themselves. When people talk about young workers and AI, they forget that we are somebody's daughter and somebody's help.

headlineQuote: A lot of people my age are carrying a family, not just themselves.
portrait: Maya Reyes is **22**, a junior developer at a regional bank in San Antonio, renting a room from her cousin.
She's the first in her family at university, owes about **ten thousand** and sends two hundred dollars home each month.
She's traditional and steady: faith and family guide her, and she uses **AI now and then**, once it's proven.
Her moods run from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year world, where her fear is mixed with shame.
Across scenarios, her plan is the **parents**: a house deposit, compliance work and a growing safety fund.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have **no time** to look after her parents and herself.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest** bank, free training, a community that stands together and quick, respectful government help.
